seed_fact: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system and possesses a powerful magnetic field.
A day on Venus is longer than a year on Venus due to its extremely slow retrograde rotation.
Saturn has thousands of individual ringlets composed primarily of water ice and rock.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest known shield volcano in the solar system.
The Sun accounts for approximately 99.86 percent of the total mass of the solar system.
Mercury experiences temperature swings ranging from minus 180 Celsius at night to 430 Celsius during the day.
Titan is Saturn's largest moon and the only moon in the solar system known to possess a dense nitrogen atmosphere.
Europa harbors a subsurface liquid water ocean beneath its icy crust that may contain more water than Earth's oceans.
The Kuiper Belt extends from Neptune's orbit out to approximately 50 astronomical units from the Sun.
The Oort Cloud is a theoretical spherical cloud of predominantly icy planetesimals surrounding the solar system up to 100000 AU.
The universe is estimated to be approximately 13.8 billion years old based on cosmic microwave background measurements.
Dark energy is responsible for the accelerating expansion rate of the observable universe.
Dark matter accounts for roughly 27 percent of the universe's total mass-energy density but does not emit or absorb light.
The Cosmic Microwave Background radiation is the thermal remnant echo of the Big Bang dating back to recombination.
The observable universe has an estimated diameter of approximately 93 billion light-years.
A supernova is the catastrophic explosion of a massive star at the culmination of its stellar evolution cycle.
Neutron stars are extraordinarily dense stellar remnants composed primarily of closely packed neutrons.
Pulsars are highly magnetized rotating neutron stars that emit focused beams of electromagnetic radiation.
Betelgeuse is a red supergiant star in Orion that is expected to explode as a core-collapse supernova.
The core of the Sun converts 600 million metric tons of hydrogen into helium every second via nuclear fusion.
White dwarfs are supported against gravitational collapse exclusively by electron degeneracy pressure.
Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky as seen from Earth with an apparent magnitude of minus 1.46.
The event horizon of a black hole represents the boundary beyond which nothing not even light can escape.
Sagittarius A star is the supermassive black hole located at the dynamical center of the Milky Way galaxy.
The first direct radio image of a black hole silhouette was captured for the supermassive black hole in galaxy M87.
Gravitational waves from colliding binary black holes were first directly detected on September 14 2015.
Hawking radiation is theoretical thermal radiation predicted to be emitted by black holes due to quantum gravitational effects.
Proxima Centauri b is the closest known rocky exoplanet orbiting within the habitable zone of our nearest stellar neighbor.
The TRAPPIST-1 system contains seven Earth-sized terrestrial planets orbiting an ultra-cool red dwarf star.
Hot Jupiters are gas giant exoplanets with orbital periods shorter than 10 days orbiting perilously close to their host stars.
WASP-76b is an ultra-hot gas giant where iron is vaporized on the day side and condenses as iron rain on the night side.
Exoplanet transit spectroscopy allows astronomers to determine atmospheric chemical composition during orbital eclipses.
The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy containing an estimated 100 to 400 billion stars.
The Andromeda Galaxy is the nearest major spiral galaxy to the Milky Way and is on a collision course in roughly 4.5 billion years.
The Large Magellanic Cloud and Small Magellanic Cloud are dwarf satellite galaxies orbiting the Milky Way.
Active Galactic Nuclei are compact central regions of galaxies powered by accretion disks feeding supermassive black holes.
The Hubble Deep Field revealed thousands of distant young galaxies in an apparently empty region of the northern sky.
Gravitational lensing occurs when massive galactic clusters bend and magnify light from more distant background galaxies.
The James Webb Space Telescope uses a 6.5 meter gold-coated beryllium primary mirror to observe in the infrared spectrum.
The Voyager 1 spacecraft launched in 1977 and became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space in 2012.
The Perseverance rover is actively caching Martian rock samples in Jezero Crater to search for signs of ancient microbial life.
The Parker Solar Probe travels closer to the Sun's corona than any previous mission reaching speeds exceeding 600000 km/h.
The New Horizons spacecraft flew past Pluto in July 2015 revealing active nitrogen glaciers and water ice mountains.
The Hubble Space Telescope was deployed into low Earth orbit in April 1990 by Space Shuttle Discovery.
Enceladus possesses global subsurface oceans that erupt through cryogenic geysers in its south polar tiger stripe fractures.
The asteroid belt resides between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter containing millions of rocky bodies including Ceres.
Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt and is classified as a dwarf planet.
Comet 67P Churyumov-Gerasimenko was orbited and landed on by the Rosetta mission revealing an organic-rich surface.
Triton is Neptune's largest moon and orbits in a retrograde direction suggesting it was a captured Kuiper Belt dwarf planet.
Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system and is the only known moon with its own internally generated magnetic field.
